templates.text: The visual pathway is undergoing robust myelination, supporting the infant's emerging ability to track high-contrast patterns.
Myelination proceeds normally along the visual pathway, enhancing signal transmission from the retina to the occipital cortex.
The optic radiations show a normal rate of myelination, crucial for the development of visual acuity.
The geniculostriate visual pathway is prioritized for myelination, facilitating the processing of form and motion.
Myelination of the visual pathway is on schedule, strengthening the neural circuits for binocular vision.
The occipital cortex receives increasingly myelinated visual input, sharpening the infant's perception of edges and shapes.
Normal myelination of the optic nerve and tract underpins the pupillary light reflex and basic visual orientation.
The dorsal visual stream, involved in spatial processing, is myelinating at the expected developmental pace.
Myelination advances along the ventral visual stream, supporting the future recognition of faces and objects.
The primary visual cortex shows a normal progression of myelination, organizing the initial map of the visual world.
The infant's visual pathway myelinates efficiently, reducing signal latency and improving contrast sensitivity.
Myelination of the lateral geniculate nucleus connections proceeds normally, refining visual information before cortical processing.
The superior colliculus pathway, mediating reflexive visual orientation, is myelinating appropriately for this stage.
Normal visual pathway myelination allows for more coordinated eye movements and sustained fixation.
The infant's visual system benefits from timely myelination, which stabilizes the transmission of pattern and light information.
Myelination of the optic chiasm and beyond proceeds on schedule, supporting the integration of visual fields.
The parvocellular visual pathway, dedicated to fine detail and color, is undergoing normal myelination.
The magnocellular visual pathway, responsible for motion detection, shows appropriate myelination for gestational age.
Myelination of the visual association areas is progressing, laying groundwork for complex visual perception.
The infant's visual tracking improves as myelination of the cortical eye fields advances normally.
Normal myelination along the visual pathway reduces neural noise, allowing clearer perception of the caregiver's face.
The retino-geniculo-cortical visual circuit demonstrates robust and timely myelination.
Myelination of the visual pathway is a priority, enabling faster processing of looming stimuli and promoting alertness.

The infant's visual system shows typical myelination, which is foundational for future visuomotor coordination.
Myelination proceeds apace in the visual cortex, organizing the columnar architecture for orientation selectivity.
The normal myelination of the visual pathway underlies the infant's growing preference for human faces.
The trans-synaptic myelination of visual cortical connections is occurring as expected, refining neural networks.
Myelination of the visual pathway enhances the signal-to-noise ratio, making salient features in the environment more distinct.
The infant's visual attention span lengthens as myelination of frontal eye field connections continues normally.
